periods.activity_title: Reading Abbakka's Story: Courage and Sovereignty

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.206): riddle warm-up and women warriors discussion.
Let us think and reflect (p.214–215): meaning of 'tribute' and sovereignty fill-in.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.213–214): cause-and-effect table based on the story.

time_bands.activity: Open with the riddle from "Let us read" (p.206): read it aloud and invite students to guess the warrior queen described. Take two or three responses, then reveal the answer and introduce the chapter's subject, Rani Abbakka of Ullal.

Conduct an unhurried teacher-led read-aloud of the narrative, pausing at key moments — Abbakka's refusal of tribute, her midnight counter-attack, and her capture. Students follow in their textbooks (pp.206–213).

Pose the prompt from "Let us read" (p.206): ask students to name other women warriors who shaped India's history, drawing on what they know. Invite brief paired exchanges, then open to the class for two or three contributions.

Move to "Let us think and reflect" (p.214–215): ask students what the word 'tribute' means as the Portuguese envoy uses it, and then take up the fill-in prompt — students complete the sentence explaining why Abbakka declares Ullal a sovereign country. Discuss responses whole-class.

periods.teacher_notes: Abbakka's defiance of the Portuguese tribute demand is the moral and dramatic centre of this narrative — draw students' attention to the word 'sovereign' and the pride it carries for the people of Ullal. A common difficulty is conflating 'sovereign country' with simple independence; the prose_summary shows Abbakka's argument is also economic, tied to the Arabic trade she establishes. The cause-and-effect table from "Let us discuss" (p.213–214) has not been covered in class; flag it as a self-study activity for students to attempt on their own using the table on page 214.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Rani Gaidinliu; Pronouncing Key Vocabulary

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.220): bio-table completion while listening to the talk on Rani Gaidinliu.
Let us speak (p.221): paired pronunciation practice for multisyllabic story vocabulary.

time_bands.activity: Distribute or direct students to the bio-table for Rani Gaidinliu on page 220. Explain that they will fill in each field as they listen, so they should scan the table now to know what details to listen for.

Read the teacher's talk about Rani Gaidinliu (p.224) aloud at a steady pace, pausing briefly after each key fact. Students complete the bio-table fields — date of birth, place, tribe, movement, arrest details, titles, awards, and honours — as the information is given.

Review the bio-table whole-class: call on individual students for each field and write correct answers on the board. Address any blank or incorrect cells by rereading the relevant sentence from the talk.

Shift to "Let us speak" (p.221): display or read out the seven words — vassal, successor, rash, league, wrath, seize, resolve. Model each pronunciation using the notes given, emphasising the stressed syllable and silent letter in 'wrath'. Students then practise in pairs, taking turns to say each word and correct each other.

periods.teacher_notes: The bio-table for Rani Gaidinliu covers specific dates, titles and award names that students may mishear; a slow, deliberate read with brief pauses after each fact helps accuracy. For the pronunciation activity, note that 'seize' and 'size' are a common confusion — the prose_summary highlights this pair — so model both together and let students hear the contrast before paired practice begins.

periods.activity_title: Writing a Conversation; Spelling and Reported Speech

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.221): guided conversation on women's role in India's identity.
Let us learn (p.215): 'ie'/'ei' spelling rule fill-in exercise.
Let us learn (p.219): rewrite sentences from direct to indirect speech.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.216): look up 'laugh' expressions and use each in an original sentence.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the spelling rule from "Let us learn" (p.215): 'i before e except after c'. Write the rule on the board and show how it applies to story words such as 'seize', 'sovereign', 'their', and 'soldiers'. Highlight the exceptions so students do not over-apply the rule.

Students work individually on the ten-blank 'ie'/'ei' fill-in exercise (p.215). After a quick paired check, review answers on the board, asking students to explain why each word follows or breaks the rule.

Introduce direct-to-indirect speech from "Let us learn" (p.219): explain the three changes — tense back-shift, pronoun shift, and time expression change — using a sentence from the Abbakka narrative as a demonstration. Students then rewrite the first three sentences in the exercise individually.

Launch the writing task from "Let us write" (p.221): students write a conversation between Pratap and Tarana discussing women's role in India's identity, using the opening lines provided. They draft six to eight sentences per character, working independently.

Students exchange drafts with a partner for a quick peer read; one partner notes one thing the conversation does well and one place where a sentence could be clearer. Two pairs share their conversations aloud with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The 'ie'/'ei' rule has well-known exceptions ('seize', 'their', 'sovereign' all appear in the Abbakka text itself) — use these story words throughout so the grammar remains rooted in what students have read. For the indirect speech sentences, the most frequent error at this stage is forgetting to back-shift the tense when the reporting verb is in the past; draw attention to this before students begin. The two remaining indirect speech sentences and the paragraph transformation (p.219–220) are not covered in class; they may be attempted independently.

periods.activity_title: Silent Letters, Word Meanings, and Group Research Presentation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.216): silent-letter word exploration and sharing findings with class.
Let us explore (p.222): group research and in-class presentation on a brave woman.

time_bands.activity: Open with 'wrath' from the Abbakka narrative — point out the silent 'w'. Ask students individually to think of three words with silent letters, using the examples from "Let us learn" (p.216) as a starting point (campaign, knowledge, pneumonia, honour, calm). Students jot their words in notebooks.

Students share their silent-letter words in pairs, then a quick whole-class round collects new examples on the board. Briefly discuss the pattern — silent letters often signal etymology — without requiring deep linguistic analysis.

Introduce the "Let us explore" project task (p.222): groups of five choose one brave woman from the list or suggest their own. Each group divides the five research headings — Childhood, Training or Education, Achievements, Contributions, and What we learn from her — among members and gathers information from memory or the textbook.

Groups present their findings to the class in an oral round; each member speaks to their assigned heading. After each presentation, the class offers one observation about what made that woman's contribution significant.

periods.teacher_notes: Silent letters in English often reflect the word's origin — Greek for 'pneumonia', Latin for 'honour' — and sharing this lightly enriches the word-building discussion without overloading the activity. For the project presentations, students work from memory and the textbook; remind them that depth on even two or three headings is more valuable than a thin sweep of all five. The match-words exercise from "Let us discuss" (p.213) that was set as self-study earlier in the chapter is worth revisiting briefly if time allows before presentations begin.

items.item_stem: When the Portuguese envoy arrived at Ullal demanding the annual tribute, Rani Abbakka declared that Ullal was a sovereign country. Which of the following best explains what she meant by calling Ullal 'sovereign' in that moment?

options.label: A
options.text: Ullal had a stronger army than Portugal and could refuse on military grounds.

options.label: B
options.text: Ullal had already paid its tribute for the year and owed nothing more.

options.label: C
options.text: Ullal was a self-governing kingdom that owed no tribute to a foreign power.

options.label: D
options.text: Ullal was protected by the Zamorin of Kozhikode and therefore untouchable.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests the student reads the refusal as a bookkeeping matter rather than a political stand on independence.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Conflates the alliance with the Zamorin — formed later — with the basis of Abbakka's sovereignty argument.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reduces Abbakka's declaration to military strength rather than the right of self-governance she asserts.

items.item_stem: Abbakka's husband Veera Narsimha called her decision to defy the Portuguese 'rash', yet the people of Ullal and her soldiers rallied behind her cause. What does this contrast between Veera Narsimha's reaction and the people's support reveal about Abbakka's leadership? Write your answer in two or three sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The contrast suggests that while Veera Narsimha weighed the risk of open defiance against a powerful colonial force, the people of Ullal trusted Abbakka's judgement and shared her determination to protect their kingdom's sovereignty. Her ability to inspire collective support despite her husband's opposition shows a leadership rooted in the community's own desire for freedom rather than in personal authority alone.

items.source_lo: Student extracts and records specific factual information from a spoken biographical account using listen-and-respond as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Rani Gaidinliu's life: dates, tribe, Heraka movement, arrest, imprisonment, titles, and posthumous honours.
items.item_stem: Listen to the teacher's talk about Rani Gaidinliu and decide whether each of the following statements is true or false.

options.text: Gaidinliu joined the Heraka movement at the age of sixteen.
Rani Gaidinliu was born in the Tamenglong district of Manipur on 26 January 1915.
The British sentenced Gaidinliu to life imprisonment in 1932.
The then Prime Minister gave Gaidinliu the title 'Daughter of the Hills'.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the talk states she was born on 26 January 1915 in the Tamenglong district of Manipur.
2. False — she joined the Heraka movement at thirteen, not sixteen; she was arrested at sixteen.
3. True — the talk states she was arrested in 1932 and sentenced to life imprisonment.
4. True — the talk states the then Prime Minister called her 'Daughter of the Hills' and gave her the title 'Rani'.

items.item_stem: Based on the talk about Rani Gaidinliu, fill in the blanks in the paragraph below with the correct details.
items.visual_stimulus:
Detail|Answer
Gaidinliu's tribe|1. ___________
Year she was released from prison|2. ___________
Award she received in 1982|3. ___________
Honour created for her in Silchar, Assam|4. ___________
Year the Government of India issued a postal stamp in her honour|5. ___________

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Rongmei (also known as Kabui). 2. 1947. 3. Padma Bhushan. 4. A park with a statue. 5. 1996.

items.item_stem: Your teacher will say each of the following words from the story of Rani Abbakka aloud twice. Repeat the word, mark which syllable you stressed, and briefly describe one phonetic feature of the word (such as a silent letter or an unexpected vowel sound): vassal, successor, wrath, seize.

expected_elements: Stresses the correct syllable in each two- or three-syllable word.
Identifies the silent 'w' in 'wrath' or the unusual vowel in 'seize'.
Pronunciation is clear and the vowel sounds match the guidance given.
Responds promptly without excessive hesitation between repetitions.

items.item_stem: Choose any two words from the list — vassal, successor, league, resolve — that appear in the story of Rani Abbakka. For each word, use it in a spoken sentence about Abbakka or her struggle, pronouncing it correctly and stressing the right syllable. Then explain in one spoken sentence why correct stress matters when saying that word.

expected_elements: Uses each chosen word in a sentence clearly connected to Abbakka's story.
Stresses the correct syllable as practised (e.g., VA-ssal, suhk-SEH-suh for successor).
Gives a plausible reason why misplaced stress causes confusion or misunderstanding.
Speaks at a steady pace with clear articulation throughout.

items.source_lo: Student constructs a coherent guided conversation in writing using a thematic prompt as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Conversation between Pratap and Tarana on women's contributions to India's national identity and strength.
items.item_stem: Write a short conversation of four exchanges (two turns each for Arjun and Meera) in which they discuss one woman from Indian history — real or fictional — who showed great courage. Use the opening line provided and make sure each speaker builds on what the other has said. Opening: 'Arjun: Meera, I was reading about a warrior queen last night and could not stop thinking about her bravery. Meera: Oh, tell me more — what made her so remarkable?'

expected_elements: Each character has at least two turns that connect logically to the previous line.
A specific woman is named and at least one achievement is mentioned.
Sentences are complete and punctuation of dialogue (inverted commas, commas) is used.
Vocabulary is appropriate to an informal but thoughtful conversation between students.

items.source_lo: Student constructs a coherent guided conversation in writing using a thematic prompt as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Conversation between Pratap and Tarana on women's contributions to India's national identity and strength.
items.item_stem: Imagine you are Tarana from the conversation with Pratap. You have just heard Pratap say: 'I think women like Rani Abbakka and Rani Gaidinliu showed the world that courage has no gender.' Write Tarana's response as a short paragraph of five to seven sentences in which she agrees, develops the idea with her own example of a brave woman, and adds her opinion on what young people today can learn from these women's lives.

expected_elements: Tarana's paragraph clearly agrees and extends Pratap's point, not merely restates it.
An independent example of a brave woman is introduced with at least one specific detail.
A personal opinion about lessons for young people is stated and briefly explained.
Writing flows coherently with appropriate linking words and varied sentence structure.

items.item_stem: Match each word from the story of Rani Abbakka with the spelling rule it illustrates.
items.visual_stimulus:
Word|Spelling Rule
seize|A. 'ei' after the letter 'c'
believe|B. 'ei' — exception to the 'i before e' rule
wrath|C. 'ie' follows the 'i before e' rule
receive|D. silent consonant at the start of the word

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: seize — B; believe — C; wrath — D; receive — A.

answer_key.right: B. 'ei' — exception to the 'i before e' rule
C. 'ie' follows the 'i before e' rule
D. silent consonant at the start of the word

items.item_stem: Rewrite the following sentence from the Rani Abbakka narrative in indirect speech, making all necessary changes to tense, pronouns, and reporting expressions: Rani Abbakka said to her soldiers, 'We will defend Ullal with every last drop of our courage, and the Portuguese will not seize what is ours.'

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Rani Abbakka told her soldiers that they would defend Ullal with every last drop of their courage, and that the Portuguese would not seize what was theirs.

items.source_context: Group presentation on a brave woman — childhood, education, achievements, contributions, and personal learning.
items.item_stem: Your group has chosen a brave woman to research and present to the class. Write a plan for your group's presentation that lists each of the five headings — Childhood, Training or Education, Achievements, Contributions, and What we learn from her — and under each heading notes two key points your group will cover. You do not need to write in full sentences; clear notes are fine.

expected_elements: All five headings are present and each carries at least two distinct points.
Points are factually grounded in the chosen woman's life, not generic.
Notes are clear enough for another group member to speak from.
The 'What we learn' section goes beyond admiration to name a specific value or lesson.

items.item_stem: After hearing all the groups' presentations on brave women, write a short paragraph (five to seven sentences) in which you compare the brave woman your group presented with Rani Abbakka from the chapter. In your paragraph, explain at least one way their challenges were similar and one way their responses to those challenges differed.

expected_elements: Names both women and states a specific similarity in the challenges they faced.
Identifies a clear, evidence-based difference in how each responded to her challenge.
Draws on details from the chapter about Abbakka, not only general impressions.
Paragraph is coherent with a clear opening statement and a concluding thought.
